opus-5.5.text:
I think revenue today is a lagging indicator. It tells you how well a company has captured the market that already exists. What I care more about is the slope, and whether we're positioned for the market that's about to exist.

When I look at our prospects, I ask a few questions.

First, is the technology curve on our side? In 3D generative AI, model quality has been improving very fast. Things that were impossible two years ago are usable now, and things that are barely usable now will be production-grade soon. If you're building on a curve like that, a lot of your future value doesn't show up in today's numbers.

Second, are users actually getting value, and do they come back? I look at retention and at how people use the product. Are they using it for real work, putting assets into games, prototypes, or 3D printing, or just playing with it once? Real usage compounds. A spike of curiosity doesn't.

Third, the team and the speed of iteration. A lot of my background is in building tools, from Taichi to now. What I learned is that a small, very strong team that ships fast can outrun much bigger organizations, especially early in a new technology wave. Big companies with big revenue also have a lot of existing business to protect, and that slows them down.

And honestly, I try not to compare myself too much to others. Every company is at a different stage. Comparing your year two to someone else's year ten just makes you anxious and doesn't help you make better decisions. The useful question is: are we better than we were three months ago, and are we solving a problem that will matter a lot in five years? If the answer to both is yes, I feel good about our prospects.

r001.rationale: The response calls current revenue a lagging indicator and says comparing a year-two company with a year-ten company does not help judge prospects, rejecting higher revenue alone as evidence of a worse business.

r002.rationale: It discusses team strength and iteration speed, but does not identify the company’s organizational DNA as influencing its potential to become like NVIDIA.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try not to judge it by revenue at this stage, because revenue today mostly tells you how big the existing market is, not how big the future one will be. Look at what we're doing with Taichi and with Meshy: we're betting on 3D content generation becoming something ordinary people do, not just studios with artists and engineers. That market barely exists yet in its full form, so of course the companies serving the current market look bigger.

What I actually look at is three things. First, are users coming back and making more things over time? That's the signal that we're solving a real problem rather than being a novelty. Second, is the technology curve moving in our favor? Generative models for 3D were nearly unusable two years ago, and now the quality jump every few months is dramatic. If you're positioned on a curve like that, the gap between you and incumbents can close very fast. Third, are we building the kind of team and infrastructure that compounds? Our background in high-performance computing and graphics programming means we can iterate on the whole pipeline, from the model to the rendering, which is hard to copy.

So my view is: revenue is a lagging indicator. I'd rather be early in a market that's about to grow a hundredfold than comfortable in one that's flat. There's a lot of risk in that, I won't pretend otherwise. But if we're right about where 3D creation is going, then the comparison to today's numbers won't matter much in a few years.

r001.rationale: The response says current revenue is a lagging indicator and argues that larger revenue today does not show which company will have greater future potential.

r002.rationale: It describes the team’s high-performance computing and graphics background as a hard-to-copy advantage, but does not connect that organizational background to becoming a company like NVIDIA.

astra-6.text: I think revenue today is only one snapshot. A company can be much bigger than us right now, but the question is: how fast are we improving, and how much value can we eventually create for customers? I try to look at whether our technology is getting better, whether people find it useful, and whether we’re learning quickly enough. If those things are moving in the right direction, there’s reason to be optimistic. Of course, eventually that has to translate into revenue. But I wouldn’t judge our prospects just by comparing our revenue today with someone else’s.

r001.rationale: The response says current revenue is only one snapshot and that prospects should not be judged just by comparing current revenue, rejecting the inference that higher revenue alone means the company is worse.
